options.label: All forms of matter and energy, and the structures they form
options.feedback: Correct. The universe comprises all of existence: every form of matter and energy, from sub-atomic particles to entire galactic filaments.

options.label: Only the stars and planets that we can see with the naked eye
options.feedback: That is only a tiny part. The universe includes all matter and energy, including unseen dark matter and dark energy, not just visible objects.

options.label: Only the galaxies that are close to the Milky Way
options.feedback: The universe includes every galaxy, no matter how far away, and also the space and matter between them.

options.label: Only the space between galaxies, not the galaxies themselves
options.feedback: The universe contains everything, including the galaxies, the stars, the planets, and the intergalactic space.

items.ok_line: The universe is everything that exists.
items.ko_line: The universe is more than just what you listed.
items.exp_text: The physical universe is the totality of all space and time, all that is, has been, and will be. It includes all energy and matter, such as planets, moons, stars, galaxies, and the contents of intergalactic space.

items.prompt: How long has the universe been expanding?

options.label: About 4.5 billion years
options.feedback: That is roughly the age of the Earth, not the universe. The universe has been expanding for much longer, since the Big Bang.

options.label: About 13.8 billion years
options.feedback: Correct. Cosmology has established that the universe has been expanding for 13.8 billion years, starting from the Big Bang.

options.label: About 93 billion years
options.feedback: That number is the diameter of the observable universe in light-years, not the age of the universe. The expansion has lasted 13.8 billion years.

options.label: About 377,000 years
options.feedback: That is how long after the Big Bang the first stable atoms formed, not the total time the universe has been expanding.

items.ok_line: The universe has expanded for 13.8 billion years.
items.ko_line: That figure does not match the universe's age.
items.exp_text: The universe began with the Big Bang and has been expanding ever since, currently measured at about 13.8 billion years. That is the time elapsed from the initial dense fireball to the present.

items.prompt: What event marked the beginning of the universe?

options.label: The formation of the first galaxies
options.feedback: Galaxies formed much later, after the universe had expanded and cooled. The beginning was the Big Bang.

options.label: The appearance of the first stars
options.feedback: The first stars formed about 100 to 300 million years after the beginning. The universe started with the Big Bang.

options.label: The Big Bang
options.feedback: Correct. The universe started from a dense fireball in an event called the Big Bang.

options.label: The creation of the cosmic microwave background
options.feedback: That light emerged about 377,000 years after the Big Bang. It is a later event, not the beginning itself.

items.ko_line: That happened after the universe had already begun.
items.exp_text: The universe's earliest state was extremely hot and dense, and it expanded from that state. This origin is called the Big Bang, the prevailing model for the universe's evolution.

items.prompt: What is the current diameter of the observable universe?

options.label: 13.8 billion light-years
options.feedback: That is the age of the universe in years, not the diameter of the observable universe. The diameter is about 93 billion light-years.

options.label: 46 billion light-years
options.feedback: That is the proper distance from Earth to the edge of the observable universe, not the full diameter across it.

options.label: 377,000 light-years
options.feedback: That number refers to how many years after the Big Bang the universe became transparent, not a distance across the observable universe.

options.label: 93 billion light-years
options.feedback: Correct. The observable universe's diameter is approximately 93 billion light-years.

items.ok_line: The observable universe stretches 93 billion light-years across.
items.ko_line: That figure does not match the observable universe's diameter.
items.exp_text: The observable universe is the spatial region from which light can reach us. Its diameter is about 93 billion light-years, with the edge about 46 billion light-years away from Earth.

options.label: Matter that is simply too faint to see, like dim stars
options.feedback: Dark matter is not just faint visible matter. It does not emit or absorb light at all, and it is inferred from its gravitational effects.

options.label: Another name for ordinary gas in interstellar space
options.feedback: Interstellar gas is ordinary baryonic matter and is visible. Dark matter is unseen and makes up far more of the universe.

options.label: Unseen matter that does not emit or absorb light
options.feedback: Correct. Dark matter is matter that does not interact with light, and its existence is discovered through its gravitational effects on matter and light.

options.label: The same as dark energy
options.feedback: They are different. Dark matter is matter that clumps and pulls things together, while dark energy is a mysterious energy that accelerates the universe's expansion.

items.ok_line: Dark matter is matter that light cannot reveal.
items.ko_line: That is not what dark matter is.
items.exp_text: Dark matter is matter that does not emit or absorb light, so it is invisible. It has been discovered because its gravity affects visible matter and light, and it makes up about 25.8% of the universe's mass and energy.

options.label: Energy stored in dark matter
options.feedback: Dark energy is not a form of dark matter's energy. It is a separate, mysterious energy that does not clump like matter.

options.label: A mysterious energy responsible for the acceleration of the universe's expansion
options.feedback: Correct. Dark energy is a mysterious form of energy that drives the expansion of the universe to accelerate.

options.label: The energy released when stars explode
options.feedback: That is a type of ordinary energy from stellar events, not the dark energy that fills the universe and causes expansion to speed up.

options.label: The same as the cosmic microwave background
options.feedback: The cosmic microwave background is light left over from recombination, not dark energy. Dark energy is what accelerates cosmic expansion.

items.ok_line: Dark energy speeds up cosmic expansion.
items.ko_line: Dark energy is not any known ordinary energy.
items.exp_text: Dark energy is a mysterious form of energy whose density stays constant over time. It began to dominate the universe's behavior after about 9.8 billion years, and it is what makes the expansion of the universe accelerate.

items.prompt: What percentage of the universe's mass and energy is ordinary (baryonic) matter?

options.label: About 100%
options.feedback: Ordinary matter is only a tiny fraction. Most of the universe is made of dark matter and dark energy.

options.label: About 25.8%
options.feedback: That is the share of dark matter, not ordinary baryonic matter. Ordinary matter is much less.

options.label: About 69.2%
options.feedback: That is the share of dark energy, not ordinary matter. Ordinary matter is only a few percent.

options.label: About 4.84%
options.feedback: Correct. Ordinary baryonic matter composes only about 4.84% of the universe's mass and energy.

items.ok_line: Ordinary matter is only a small fraction.
items.ko_line: That percentage belongs to something else.
items.exp_text: In the ΛCDM model, ordinary baryonic matter makes up only about 4.84% of the universe's mass and energy. Dark matter is about 25.8%, and dark energy about 69.2%.

items.prompt: At the very largest scale, how are galaxies distributed in the universe?

options.label: In a single long line
options.feedback: The large-scale distribution is not a line. Galaxies are spread across the universe in a foam-like structure of filaments and voids.

options.label: Scattered randomly with no pattern
options.feedback: The distribution is not random. It appears uniform at the largest scale, but on smaller scales it forms clusters and filaments.

options.label: Uniformly and the same in all directions
options.feedback: Correct. At the largest scale, galaxies are distributed uniformly and the same in all directions.

options.label: Grouped into one giant cluster at the center
options.feedback: The universe has no center. Galaxies are spread throughout, with no privileged location.

items.ok_line: At huge scales, galaxies are evenly spread.
items.ko_line: That is not how galaxies are arranged at the largest scale.
items.exp_text: The universe is isotropic and homogeneous at the largest scales, meaning galaxies look the same in every direction and are evenly distributed. On smaller scales, however, they gather into clusters and superclusters.

items.prompt: What structure do galaxies form at intermediate scales, between clusters and the largest scale?

options.label: Filaments and voids
options.feedback: Correct. Galaxies are arranged in clusters and superclusters that form immense filaments, with large empty voids between them, creating a foam-like structure.

options.label: A single flat sheet
options.feedback: The arrangement is not a flat sheet. It is a three-dimensional web of filaments and voids.

options.label: A spherical shell
options.feedback: There is no spherical shell structure. The distribution is a foam-like network of filaments and voids.

options.label: Pairs of galaxies only
options.feedback: Galaxies also form clusters and superclusters, not just pairs. These larger groupings make up filaments and voids.

items.ok_line: Galaxies form filaments around empty voids.
items.ko_line: That is not the structure of galaxy distribution.
items.exp_text: At intermediate scales, galaxies are not uniformly spread. They are found in clusters and superclusters, which line up into long filaments, while vast regions called voids contain very few galaxies. This makes a foam-like structure across the universe.
